Use the subjunctive after the same verbs in the negative and (optionally) the interrogative.

Tuesday, 14 October 2031. After the elections, a new minister has been appointed to Culture. His adviser, Mr Lenoir, receives Julien in Paris. The ministry wants to make savings, and the “Musique en partage” network is on the list.
Mr Moreau, I’ll be frank. The new minister thinks the network costs too much. He thinks the money would be more useful elsewhere.
I don’t think the minister has read our report. Twelve orchestras, seven hundred children and a budget smaller than that of a single festival.
He has read it. But he doubts the results are measurable. Where is the profitability?
It seems to me you are asking the wrong question. I don’t think you can measure a child who opens their eyes on hearing a waltz.
That’s very nice, Mr Moreau. But I’m not sure it’s a budgetary argument.
Then here are some figures. In Lille, absenteeism has fallen by eighteen percent. In Marseille, three children got into the Conservatoire. Nobody can deny that these are results.
I don’t deny it’s interesting. But it seems the minister wants to group all music projects into a single programme.
Do you really think that’s a saving? I’m convinced that in two years everything will have to start over and it will cost twice as much.
(sighs) I confess I’m not sure the minister is right. But I’m not the one who decides.
Then let me talk to him. Ten minutes. I’m sure he’ll understand.
I doubt he has ten minutes before December. But I’ll try. I promise nothing.
Thank you. And please take him this. It’s a recording. A sailor playing the harmonica, in Dakar, in 1978. I think it’s worth all the figures.
When you ARE SURE of what you say, you use the indicative. This applies to penser, croire, trouver, être sûr, être certain, être persuadé, il me semble, il est évident:
It is obvious that the children are making progress.
The typical mistake of advanced learners: subjunctive everywhere after “penser”. “Je pense qu’il soit…” ✗ → “Je pense qu’il est…”. The subjunctive only appears in the negative!
In the negative, the opinion becomes a DOUBT, so the verb switches to the subjunctive:
Je ne pense pas que ce soit juste.
Je crois qu’on peut le mesurer.
Je ne crois pas qu’on puisse le mesurer.
Je suis sûr qu’il a lu le rapport.
Je ne suis pas sûr qu’il ait lu le rapport.
Il n’est pas certain qu’il vienne.
Romanian makes a similar distinction only sometimes (“nu cred să vină” / “nu cred că vine”). In French the rule is much stricter, especially in writing.
In questions with inversion (careful register), you can use the subjunctive to express doubt:
Do you really think it’s a saving? (I doubt it)
Do you think he can come?
Do you think he’ll come? (spoken, no inversion → indicative)
In speech, with “est-ce que” or intonation, the indicative is almost always used. The subjunctive in a question is a sign of elevated register.
4. Il me semble que ≠ il semble que
Il me semble que vous avez tort.
Il semble que le ministre veuille faire des économies.
A single pronoun (“me”) changes the mood! It is one of the favourite traps in the DELF B2 exam.
Je doute qu’il ait dix minutes.
Personne ne peut nier que ce soient des résultats.
Je conteste que ce soit une économie.
Il est peu probable qu’il change d’avis.
Ce n’est pas que je sois contre, mais…
Careful: “ne pas douter que” (= to be sure) can be followed by the indicative: “Je ne doute pas qu’il viendra.” But the subjunctive is also correct in writing.
I don’t think it can be measured.
“It seems to me you are wrong.”

The weeks after Odile’s death had been strange. Life went on, as it always does, but something was missing from the building on rue d’Austerlitz. In the morning, at seven, no door opened any more on the other side of the landing. There was no voice whistling the next three notes. There was only Rose-Hélène, who kept crossing the landing with her key on its blue ribbon.

She would go into the empty flat, stand in the middle of the living room, play the three notes on the harmonica, then whistle the next three. Then she would come back, satisfied, to have her breakfast. Ioana had wondered whether it was healthy. She had talked about it with the nursery psychologist. The psychologist had smiled. “I don’t think it’s a problem,” she had said. “Quite the opposite. She has found her own way of saying goodbye. Let her be.”

On Thursday 4 September, Rose-Hélène had started nursery school for the first time, on rue Dumenge, two hundred metres from home. She was three and a half. She had insisted on taking Henri’s harmonica in her school bag, next to her cuddly toy. Julien had tried to explain that school is no place for musical instruments. She had looked at him as if he had said something outrageous.

Her teacher, Mrs Chevalier, a woman of about fifty with short hair, had discovered the harmonica on the very first day. Instead of confiscating it, she had asked Rose-Hélène to play something for the class. Rose-Hélène had played the three notes. Then she had explained, very seriously, to some twenty-five three-year-olds, that it was a sailor’s waltz and that you had to leave a silence for those who are no longer here.

Mrs Chevalier had phoned Ioana that very evening. “I don’t know what’s going on in your family,” she had said, “but your daughter has just given the most beautiful music lesson I have ever heard. Could you explain?” It had taken Ioana an hour to tell her everything. At the end, Mrs Chevalier had asked whether she could learn the waltz with the whole class.

Henri-Ion was nine months old and had discovered that he could get around. Not walking, not yet, but on all fours, at impressive speed. His favourite destination was the flat’s door, always open, and beyond it the landing, and further still Odile’s door. He would stop in front of it, sit down and wait. Nobody knew what he was waiting for. But he always waited in the same place.

At the end of September, Lucia had announced some news at a family dinner. She had waited until everyone was seated, the glasses were full, and Radu had finished telling an endless story from the building site. Then she had put down her fork. “I’m pregnant,” she had said. “The baby is due in May.” Radu, who already knew, had looked at his sister. Ioana had dropped her glass.

“In May,” Ioana had repeated, when she found her voice again. “The month of birthdays.” Lucia had laughed. “I know. But I don’t think you can choose.” That very evening Ioana had phoned their mother in Iași. Elena had cried for twenty minutes, then started a new list. Grandma had said she already knew. She had dreamt of fish again.

At the beginning of October the bad news had begun. After the summer elections a new government had been formed. The new Minister of Culture, Arnaud Desforges, a fifty-year-old former banker, had announced a vast savings plan. In a radio interview he had declared that he didn’t think the state could keep funding “dozens of small scattered projects”.

Amina had heard the interview live, at the office in Croix-Rousse. She had immediately opened a new spreadsheet, titled “Threat”. Then she had called Julien, who was at La Duchère. “I’m not sure we are targeted,” she had said. “But it seems to me we should get ready.” Julien had understood. When Amina said “it seems to me”, it meant she was already sure.

On 10 October an official letter had arrived from the ministry. It was polite, short and icy. The “Musique en partage” network was to be “re-examined as part of the general review of cultural spending”. A decision would be taken before the end of the year. Julien’s contract, which was due to be renewed in July, was suspended until further notice.

Julien had read the letter three times, standing in the kitchen. Then he had put it on the table, next to the calendar, and stayed silent for a long time. Ioana had found him there when she came back from the office. She had read the letter too. “I don’t think they’ll go through with it,” she had said. “Twelve cities, seven hundred children. They won’t dare.” Julien hadn’t answered. He wasn’t sure at all.

On 14 October he had got a meeting at the ministry in Paris, with the new minister’s adviser, Mr Lenoir. The interview had lasted forty minutes. Lenoir had been polite, frank and desperately reasonable. He did not deny that the network had results. But he doubted these results were “measurable”, and the minister believed only in figures.

At the end, Julien had left him a copy of the Dakar recording on a USB stick. Lenoir had taken it with a polite smile, without conviction. On the train home, Julien had watched the fields of Burgundy go by, grey and wet under the October rain. He was thinking of Odile. He wondered what she would have said. He was almost sure she would have said: “Don’t worry. Whistle.”

During those weeks of uncertainty, Théo and Lucia had carried on with rehearsals as if nothing had happened. They didn’t want the children to worry. But the children knew. Children always know. Yanis had asked Théo whether they would have to give back the instruments. Sami no longer spoke at all. And Inès, who was now fourteen, had declared that she didn’t believe a minister could understand music, since he had never played any.

Yves Le Goff had called from Nantes as soon as he heard the news. He was furious. “I don’t think this minister has ever seen the sea,” he had growled. “Otherwise he’d know you don’t cut down a mast in the middle of a storm.” Then he had offered to go to Paris himself, with his cane and his crêpe pan, to make the minister taste galettes. Julien had thanked him. He had kept the idea in reserve.

That’s exactly what they had done. The idea had come from Inès, at a Wednesday rehearsal, when Théo had explained to the children that the orchestra might disappear. She had raised her hand. “Sir, what if we recorded the waltz, with Odile’s silence, and sent it to the minister? All the orchestras. All twelve. On the same day.” Théo had looked at Lucia. Lucia had smiled.

Amina had organised everything in ten days. On Saturday 1 November, at eleven o’clock sharp, the network’s twelve orchestras had played Henri’s waltz at the same time, each in its own city, in front of its own lime tree. In Lille, Strasbourg, Marseille, Toulouse, Nantes, Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux, Rennes, Nice, Dijon, Paris and in the little Corsican village above Corte, where Antoine had sung with the three singers.

And at La Duchère, in front of the Salle Hélène Morel, under the lime tree where a handful of Odile’s ashes rested, Théo’s orchestra had played too. At the third verse, as in the other eleven cities, all the children had stopped at the same moment. Eight bars of silence. And in every city someone had whistled. At La Duchère, Rose-Hélène.

Marc Delorme, who still wrote for the neighbourhood paper, had edited the twelve videos together. You could see the twelve orchestras, the twelve lime trees, the twelve silences and the twelve people whistling: an old Corsican shepherd, a headmistress from Lille, a Marseille saxophonist, a three-year-old girl in Lyon. He had titled the video “Odile’s Silence”. He had published it that same evening.

In one week the video had been viewed two million times. The TV news had talked about it. Orchestras in other countries had started playing the waltz with eight bars of silence, without even knowing who Odile had been. In Seville, don Manuel had played it on the guitar in front of the cathedral. In Iași, Grandma had whistled the third verse in front of her gate, filmed by a neighbour.

Claire Vasseur had published an op-ed in a major national newspaper. In it she explained that she didn’t think the ministry’s decision was reasonable, that it seemed to her the debate was badly framed, and that she doubted an educational project could be judged like a business. She ended by inviting the minister to come and listen. It was unlikely, she wrote, that he would leave with the same opinion.

Support had come from everywhere. Mrs Keller, the mayor of Strasbourg, had written to the Prime Minister. Mr Benhamou had organised a support concert in the Vieux-Port. Mrs Vandamme had collected the signatures of all the parents in Lille on a petition. And, to everyone’s surprise, Bernard Delorme, the former opponent of the La Duchère hall, had taken the floor in the Lyon city council.

“Two years ago,” he had said, “I voted against this project. I thought it was money thrown out of the window. I no longer think so. I was wrong. And I’m convinced the minister is wrong today, as I was wrong yesterday. I propose that the city of Lyon write officially to the ministry.” The motion had been passed unanimously. Even the opposition had raised their hands.

Mrs Roux, in Villeurbanne, had done something nobody expected. She had written the minister a handwritten letter, three pages long. In it she told of Lucien, the brass band, the clarinet, the trip to Paris. She concluded: “Minister, I am eighty-five years old. It seems to me I have the right to tell you that you are mistaken. I doubt you will answer me. But I wanted you to know.” She had received a reply two weeks later, signed by the minister’s own hand.

On 25 November, Mr Lenoir had phoned Julien. His voice had changed. It was less polite and more human. “The minister has seen the video,” he had said. “His daughter showed it to him. She’s twelve. She plays the violin. He has also listened to the Dakar recording. I’m not sure he will change his mind. But he agrees to come. On 3 December. Ten minutes.”

Ten minutes. Julien had spent a week wondering what you can say in ten minutes to a man who believed only in figures. Amina had prepared him a forty-page file with coloured charts. Claire Vasseur had written him a speech. Théo had proposed a twenty-minute musical programme. Julien had thanked them all, then put everything aside.

On Wednesday 3 December, at two in the afternoon, a black car had stopped in front of the Salle Hélène Morel. It was cold. The lime tree had no leaves left. Minister Desforges had got out, with Lenoir and two assistants. He was a tall, thin man with narrow glasses, who looked at his watch as he walked. Julien was waiting for him alone in front of the door. He had shaken his hand without saying anything.

He hadn’t made him go in straight away. He had first taken him to the lime tree. He had shown him the plaque on the façade: “Salle Hélène Morel. She waited all her life. Thanks to her, children will wait no more.” Then he had shown him, hanging from a low branch, Lucien Roux’s old clarinet reed, swaying in the wind. The minister had asked what it was.

Julien had told him. Lucien Roux, the Villeurbanne brass band, the clarinet given to Inès, the trip to Paris, the reed Mrs Roux had given Odile and that Odile had given back “for the tree”. The minister had listened without looking at his watch. Then he had asked who Odile was. Julien had looked at his watch. Seven minutes left. He had decided he would not talk about the budget.

Inside, the sixty children were waiting, seated, in silence, with their instruments. Théo was standing in front of them. Lucia was at the back of the hall, her hand on her rounded belly. In the front row, next to an empty armchair covered with a blue shawl, sat Rose-Hélène with her harmonica, and Isabelle, holding her hand. The minister had sat down in the second row, next to Lenoir.

Théo had nodded to Inès. Lucien Roux’s clarinet had begun alone, very softly. Then the violins, then Yanis’s red cello, then Sami’s flute, then the whole orchestra. Henri’s waltz had filled the hall, under the big skylight through which the grey December light fell. The minister didn’t move. He had taken off his glasses.

At the third verse, the sixty children had stopped at the same moment. Eight bars of silence. And Rose-Hélène had stood up, in front of the empty armchair, and whistled. Off-key, breathy, as always. The minister had looked at the little girl, then at the empty armchair, then at the blue shawl. Lenoir had seen his jaw clench. When the orchestra started again, the minister had looked away.

After the waltz, Inès had walked up to the minister, clarinet in hand. Nobody had asked her to. “Minister,” she had said, “I don’t think you know who Odile was. She was a lady who whistled. The silence is her place. We keep it for her. If you abolish the orchestra, nobody will keep it for her any more.” Then she had gone back to her seat, sitting very straight.

The minister had stayed two hours. He had asked to meet the children, one by one. He had asked Yanis how to hold a bow. He had asked Sami to play him something on the flute. He had asked Rose-Hélène to lend him her harmonica. She had thought for a long time, then agreed, on condition that he gave it back. He had blown into it. A wrong note. Everyone had laughed.

Before leaving, in the cold, in front of the leafless lime tree, the minister had taken Julien aside. “I promise you nothing, Mr Moreau,” he had said. “I’m not sure my departments will understand. But I doubt this can be abolished. It even seems to me it should be extended.” He had put his glasses back on. “My daughter plays the violin, you know. She’d like to learn the waltz too.”

The decision had come on 19 December. The “Musique en partage” network was not abolished. It was maintained, with a slightly increased budget, and would be extended to twenty cities in 2033. Julien’s contract was renewed for three years. Amina had read the official statement aloud at the office, without any emotion. Then she had closed her office door. For the second time.

On the evening of the decision, Radu had spread a large map of France on the kitchen table. With a red pencil he had circled eight possible new cities: Grenoble, Montpellier, Lille-Roubaix, Le Havre, Metz, Limoges, Brest, Avignon. “Eight new halls,” he had said, his eyes shining. “Eight skylights.” Lucia had put her hand on her belly. “Start with the baby’s room,” she had replied. “The halls can come afterwards.”

Grandma had arrived from Iași on 22 December, on Costel’s coach, with her usual cool box. She was eighty-five. Getting off the coach at Perrache, she had asked where Odile was. Nobody had dared tell her on the phone. Ioana had broken the news to her there, in the car park, in the sleet. Grandma had said nothing. She had only made the sign of the cross, then asked to be taken straight to rue d’Austerlitz.

On 23 December, Odile would have turned eighty-one. The whole family had gathered in her flat, around the empty armchair, by the window looking out on Fourvière. Isabelle had made an apple tart, her mother’s only recipe. Yves Le Goff had sent a parcel of galettes from Nantes. Elena and Dan had come from Iași for Christmas, with Grandma, who had crossed Europe by coach once more.

Nobody made speeches. At the end of the meal, Rose-Hélène had stood up, taken her harmonica and placed herself in front of the empty armchair. She had played the three notes. Then she had whistled the next three. Then she had fallen silent and waited. Eight bars of silence, in Odile’s living room, with the whole family around.

And in that silence, Henri-Ion, sitting on the floor in front of the door, in the spot where he always stopped, had done something he had never done before. He had started to whistle. Well, to blow rather, making a noise with his lips that sounded like no note at all. But he was blowing, very seriously, looking at the empty armchair. Grandma had crossed herself. Isabelle had burst into sobs.

Julien had looked at his son, then at his daughter, then at the armchair, then at the window where the lights of Fourvière were shining. He remembered Odile’s letter: “If one day you hear whistling on the other side of the landing, don’t look for who it is. Answer.” So he had answered. He had whistled the next three notes. And the whole family, in all the languages it knew, had followed him to the end.

Tribune : « La musique n’est pas une dépense »
We learn that the Ministry of Culture is considering abolishing the “Musique en partage” network. I don’t think this decision is reasonable, and I would like to explain why.
It seems to me the debate is badly framed. People ask whether the network is profitable. I doubt an educational project can be judged like a business. Nobody asks whether a school is profitable.

I am convinced the figures speak for themselves. In three years, absenteeism has fallen in all the cities involved. It is obvious that these children love school more since they have been playing in an orchestra.
It seems the ministry wants to group this network with other programmes. I don’t deny that savings are necessary. But I don’t think you save money by destroying what works.

People will object that music is a luxury. I’m not sure those who say so have ever seen a child from La Duchère playing in front of two thousand people at the Philharmonie. I have seen it. It wasn’t a luxury. It was a necessity.

I believe the minister is a man of good faith. That is why I simply ask him to come and listen. It is unlikely he will leave with the same opinion. — Claire Vasseur, director of the Lyon Conservatoire
